narrative:
The model predicted a 96% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess future success, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year in law school was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Standing in the bottom decile (compared to an average of roughly the sixth decile among accepted students) signaled persistent academic struggle. Your LSAT score was the second most important factor and also pulled the outcome toward failure; a score of 25 is well below the average of 37 seen among students who were admitted. Finally, your first-year class rank added further weight in the same direction. Placing in the lowest decile (versus an average around the sixth decile for accepted applicants) reinforced the pattern of performance that the model associates with not passing the bar.

Gender, race, family income, whether you plan to attend full-time, and your undergraduate GPA played little or no role in this particular decision.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record if you retake courses, consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score, and seek targeted bar-preparation support. These steps can directly address the areas that most influenced the current prediction. (218 words)
